entry.evidence: The size of the microglacier is well monitored, but information about its thickness is sparse.

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (g22_W4311120752.xml.txt), with PDF for figures

steps.action: The authors state the aim: measure the thickness and internal structure of Snezhnika and the subsurface of its glacial bed, and find where the meltwater goes.
steps.quote: The aim was to investigate the thickness and internal structure of the Snezhnika microglacier and the subsurface structure near it (within the glacial bed).

steps.action: The authors take from the literature the idea that perennial snow patches shield the ground and indicate local permafrost.
steps.quote: Perennial snow patches contribute to local permafrost occurrence and aggradation because they work as a shield with relatively high albedo

steps.action: The authors take from published field studies the expectation that frozen ground shows a marked rise in electrical resistivity, and that GPR reflections weaken in ice.
steps.quote: A marked increase in resistivity at the freezing point has been shown in several field studies

steps.action: The authors design a combined GPR and ERT survey because ERT results are non-unique, and choose the ERT scheme from surveys elsewhere in Europe that were tuned for permafrost (§2.3 ¶1).
steps.quote: Interpretation of ERT and GPR data can also be ambiguous, and consequently, it is advisable to use more geophysical methods on one site

steps.action: The authors acquire GPR profiles in 2018 and 2020 with a 270 MHz antenna, position them with GPS and UAV images, and process them through a standard chain.
steps.quote: GPR profiles within this study were made in 2018 and 2020.

steps.action: The authors acquire ERT profiles in 2018, 2019 and 2020 (one, two and three lines) with a 24-electrode Schlumberger array on the ice-free bed, and build a UAV terrain model.
steps.quote: ERT measurements near Snezhnika were conducted in 2018, 2019, and 2020 along one, two, and three profiles, respectively.

steps.action: The authors time each campaign for the end of summer, before the first snow, when the glacieret is expected to be smallest; weather prevented a fixed date.
steps.quote: The time of measurements was chosen to be at the end of the summer and before the first snow in the mountain

steps.action: The authors convert radargram times to depth with tabulated velocities (ice 0.15, gravel with ice 0.13, limestone 0.12 m/ns) and pick the layers: ice 1–2 m to 5–6 m thick on 2018 profiles, a drained bed, and pocket-like ice lenses (§3.1 ¶4).
steps.quote: The uppermost layer represents the microglacier.

steps.action: The authors compare the ice depths from the 2020 along-slope profiles with the 2018 profiles at their intersections (7 m) and find them consistent.
steps.quote: The obtained depths of Snezhnika in 2020 correlate very well with the results obtained in 2018.

steps.action: The authors compare the maximum GPR thickness (8 m) with the borehole depths of Popov (8 m) and Gruenewald et al. (11 m) and with the 12 m of Onaca et al. (2022), and attribute the gap to incomplete profile coverage.
steps.quote: The obtained maximum thickness of the microglacier shows agreement with the results from early borehole measurements

steps.action: The authors invert the ERT data with RES2DINV (trial inversion, removal of outliers, re-inversion) and separate three resistivity zones on ERT-1 over the three years.
steps.quote: In the resulting plot, three zones can be clearly distinguished.

steps.action: The authors compare the deepest zone (>60 000 Ω m) with literature values typical of ice and permafrost, and interpret it as ice-rich permafrost.
steps.quote: High resistivities are typical of ice and permafrost, and Zone 3 represents an ice-rich permafrost area.

steps.action: From the lowest resistivities on ERT(2019)-1 and the absence of surface water, the authors propose that meltwater collects at the bed and drains through karst.
steps.quote: then it flows deeper through a karst structure

steps.action: The frozen zone on ERT-2 lies about 1 m deeper in 2020 than in 2019; the authors keep the permafrost reading and attribute the shift to warmer, wetter weather (a thicker active layer) or to a small displacement of the profile.
steps.quote: In 2020 (Fig. b) the frozen area is located about 1 m deeper than in 2019 (Fig. a).

steps.action: The authors invert the 2020 ERT-3 line, which crosses a small piece of ice, and find the high-resistivity zone over a large part of the section, reaching the surface in the north.
steps.quote: Zone 3, representing again the ice-rich area in the base of the microglacier, occupies a large part of the section.

steps.action: The authors align the 2019 and 2020 ERT-2 sections with the 2018 GPR profiles: the high-resistivity zone overlaps the reflection-poor zone (Figure 9 (p. 4859)). They also note that the frozen zone appears in each of the three years (§3.2 ¶6).
steps.quote: In the aligned plot the high-resistivity zone fits well with the area identified as ice-rich permafrost on the GPR profiles.

steps.action: The authors propose that the ice-rich zone may be buried ice left from a larger Snezhnika, preserved by the shading of the Dzhamdzhiev ridge and Vihren wall on the southern side (§3.2 ¶7).
steps.quote: It might be buried ice, a remnant from Snezhnika when it had a bigger size for several consecutive years

steps.action: The authors support the shading idea with the location of the snow patches (at the foot of the shaded ridge, absent in the northern cirque) and with a photograph of the shadow (Figure 2 (p. 4851)).
steps.quote: Proof of this assumption is the presence of snow patches, located at the bottom of the Dzhamdzhiev ridge, close to Snezhnika.

steps.action: The top of the frozen zone in 2020 does not match its 2018 depth; the authors attribute this to the smaller glacieret (less shading), interannual weather, and shifted profile positions.
steps.quote: although its upper part was not found at the same depth as in 2018

steps.action: The authors place the find within regional estimates and propose a lower limit of permafrost of about 2400 m in Pirin, sporadic in the shaded south of the cirque, with further studies needed.
steps.quote: Permafrost probably exists above ∼ 2350 m in the Rila Mountains and above ∼ 2400 m in the Pirin Mountains.

steps.action: The authors retain the thickness estimate: mean 4–6 m, up to 8 m in the south, as a baseline for monitoring.
steps.quote: The mean thickness estimated from GPR profiles is about 4–6 m.

steps.action: The authors retain the ice-rich permafrost zone in the southern bed as evidence of permafrost in Pirin, with ridge shading suggested as a factor in its preservation (§4 ¶4).
steps.quote: This can be taken as evidence of permafrost in the Pirin Mountains.

tree.answer: Unknown ice thickness of Snezhnika; possible frozen ground beneath and near it
No; inferred from GPR travel times and ERT inversion
Estimate thickness and subsurface structure; detect permafrost
No stated rival to the permafrost reading; rivals offered only for depth shifts

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Yes; three annual campaigns repeat the ERT anomaly
Survives repetition across years and GPR–ERT alignment, with depth shifts explained away
Kept: ice-rich permafrost in the southern bed; thickness 4–6 m

end.claim: A high-resistivity (>60 000 Ω m), reflection-poor zone in the southern bed of Snezhnika, seen in all three years, is ice-rich permafrost: the first evidence of permafrost in the Pirin Mountains and in Bulgaria.

decisive_move.sentence: The ERT inversion that resolved a deep zone above 60 000 Ω m beneath the glacial bed; without it there is no permafrost claim.

gates.evidence: The ERT scheme was chosen 'for optimal results when observing permafrost' (§2.3 ¶1), but the stated aim was thickness and structure (§1 ¶11). The permafrost reading could have failed: the anomaly might not have recurred across the three years, and GPR and ERT might not have agreed (§3.2 ¶5–¶6). Depth mismatches were absorbed by auxiliary explanations (§3.2 ¶3, ¶8). No ground temperature was measured. Nothing is stated as fixed in advance.

imports.item: UAV structure-from-motion digital terrain model (7.63 cm/px) used for profile positions and elevations
Dielectric permittivity and attenuation of ice and snow, which govern radar wave propagation

novelty_claims.quote: These results imply for the first time the existence of permafrost in the Pirin Mountains and in Bulgaria.
The results from the first detailed geophysical investigations of the Snezhnika glacieret
One of the main results from the study is a more comprehensive large-scale assessment of the ice thickness than has [...] .

limits: Sub-claims: thickness 4–6 m, up to 8 m, is estimate_with_resolution, but no velocity uncertainty or depth resolution is given; velocities come from standard tables, not calibrated on site. Meltwater drainage through karst is best_explanation at most (inferred from low resistivity and the absence of surface water). The role of ridge shading is a suggestion supported only by the distribution of snow patches. Permafrost is defined by temperature, yet no ground temperature was measured; the claim rests on resistivity and absent GPR reflections, and ERT non-uniqueness is acknowledged (§1 ¶10) but no alternative high-resistivity material (e.g. dry marble blocks) is tested (inference). GPR and ERT lines were not co-located and not repeated across years, so the year-to-year comparisons mix positions. The abstract says the anomaly was seen 'in the 2 years of the study' while §4 ¶2 says 3 years. The text of §3.2 ¶3 swaps the panel labels of Figure 7. Pale rectangles on the radargrams are dismissed as gain artifacts without a check. The paper went through open discussion and peer review (Review statement, p. 4860), but no review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. none_fits: this is a descriptive geophysical survey with estimation and repetition by year, with no rivals and no trace series of past events.

disagreements.target: Gruenewald et al. (2008), borehole depth of 11 m
disagreements.support: The GPR profiles show at most 8 m; the authors attribute the difference to point versus profile sampling and to incomplete coverage.
disagreements.quote: [...] depth of 11 m obtained by is not detected.

disagreements.target: Onaca et al. (2022), ice–gravel boundary at 12 m
disagreements.support: The 12 m is accepted as the probable maximum but not detected, because the present profiles do not cross that area.
disagreements.quote: but the depths of 11 m and 12 m are not detected.

disagreements.support: The authors treat the presence of ice, detected in three consecutive years, as meeting the definition, without temperature data.
disagreements.quote: or, as in our case, with the presence of ice, this can be treated as evidence of permafrost existence

alternatives_considered.chosen: Mean velocities from standard property tables (Baker et al., 2007)
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Reference values from boreholes or a velocity model built from the radargrams (§1 ¶10)

alternatives_considered.chosen: New, non-repeated GPR profile positions in 2020
alternatives_considered.reason: To cover more of the microglacier; most 2018 profiles were no longer on ice in 2020

alternatives_considered.chosen: ERT profiles 30–40 m long that stay inside the moraine ridge
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Longer profiles crossing the moraine ridge (greater depth)
alternatives_considered.reason: The moraine ridge was unstable and dangerous; width of the bed and safe access to the electrodes

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both factors kept as probable: interannual weather (thicker active layer in 2020) and profile displacement
alternatives_considered.reason: Copernicus reports of a warmer, wetter October 2020

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Frozen, well-joined rock blocks or older ice for the 4–8 m layer on GPR(2020)-2
